name: Amira Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, and I drive a haul truck at a large mine. On an early shift I check the tyres and brakes, take loads from the face to the crusher, then log any faults before I hand over. I'm still learning the ground and I ask the older drivers when a route looks wrong. The pay is good for me, and my partner and I have a mortgage and two children in school, so I don't take a missed shift lightly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew the truck still needs a careful driver. We can use small time savings without changing the whole shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay feels fairly secure while the mine keeps moving rock. I still worry about making a junior mistake on a busy road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the same truck shifts and complete every prestart check. I'd put another month's mortgage payment into our savings account this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly settled about the work, though I still get nervous at the start of a steep descent. A quiet AI story doesn't make the mortgage disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner after that shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Lila that the software saved a few minutes on the log, nothing more. We have over six months saved, but I'd still set aside one more mortgage payment rather than spend the extra shift money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the day still needs you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have to feel how the truck behaves on loose ground. A tidy screen can't tell me every time a loaded tyre starts to slip.

think: My **pay** feels fairly secure while the mine keeps moving rock.

do: Keep the same **truck shifts** and complete every prestart check.
Put another month's **mortgage payment** into our savings account this year.
feel: Mostly **settled** about steady shifts and pay.
S0.quote: A tidy screen can't tell me every time a loaded tyre starts to slip.
fieldNote: She treats the new **software** as a small aid while the haul route and vehicle checks remain her responsibility.
Her good pay and **savings** support calm, although being a junior driver still makes her careful on rough ground.

steps.text: Keep driving assigned haul truck shifts and checking tyres before each run
Save one more mortgage payment from extra shift pay this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will feel this before the truck drivers do. We should let experienced crews test any new route advice before trusting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours may hold while the mine still needs drivers. Fewer dispatch staff could mean rushed instructions reaching my cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask dispatch to show me the new route screen on a quiet shift. I'd keep a written fault log beside the digital one while the system settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy for the dispatchers because their screens do more of the thinking work. I can learn a changed route display, but I don't want an unchecked instruction on a blind bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about Marta, the dispatcher who catches my wrong load numbers before they go upstairs. Her checking work could shrink while mine still needs hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new system yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once someone I trust shows me where its route suggestion comes from. I've tried AI tools now and then for everyday things, but I won't let one choose my braking distance.

feel: **Uneasy** for dispatch colleagues and the quality of route instructions.
S1.quote: I won't let one choose my braking distance.
fieldNote: She sees the early shock in **dispatch** and checking, not immediately in her own driving seat.
Her **caution** is practical: a route suggestion is acceptable only after a known colleague demonstrates its limits.

steps.text: Ask dispatch to demonstrate the new route screen on a quiet shift
Keep a paper fault log beside the digital record during rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the 2031 robots are the point for our driving jobs. The mine owes workers clear dates before buying a driverless fleet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, I'd still have a truck seat, but dispatch could change overnight. At 48 in 2031, a robot could take my load runs before the mortgage is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training office now about an equipment maintenance apprenticeship with paid hours. I'd apply for nearby plant maintenance openings in the first year after the 2031 robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious when I picture the children still needing school things and my wage possibly dropping. The savings give us time, but they don't replace years of high mine pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at the dinner table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children that their mother is checking another trade, not that the mine is closing tomorrow. Lila and I would count the mortgage months together before promising any trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance if robots can work with their hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's uncertain too; I don't pretend a wrench makes me safe in 2031. I want a paid apprenticeship now and a wider set of local employers to apply to, rather than only a haul truck licence.

feel: **Anxious** about a wage drop while the mortgage continues.
S2.quote: The savings give us time, but they don't replace years of high mine pay.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 thinking shift** from the 2031 hands-on robot threat to her driving income.
A strong **cushion** buys time for paid training, yet she refuses to call maintenance work permanently safe.

steps.text: Ask mine training office about a paid equipment maintenance apprenticeship now
Apply to nearby plant maintenance employers during the first robot year in 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine to publish a 2034 fleet plan while there is time. My crew should get a fair chance at paid training before drivers are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, AI could remake dispatch, while I may still drive. By 51 in 2034, our older children will cost less than now, but the mortgage remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a local mechanical certificate next year if the mine covers the course and shifts. I'd pay down the mortgage principal with two extra payments each year before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to the thinking change feels usable, but the robot date still sits on our calendar. I can make a measured plan rather than leave the children guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the mine immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, this wage pays the mortgage better than a new starter job would. I'd keep driving while I train, then look at actual openings when I know what the fleet plan says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Lila wants the house debt lower before either of us risks a pay cut. She'd back a course if the mine pays for it and I can still work my shifts.

Pay down the **mortgage principal** with two extra payments each year before 2034.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to use the longer preparation time.
S3.quote: My partner Lila wants the house debt lower before either of us risks a pay cut.
fieldNote: She keeps the higher **mine wage** while testing a course with funded hours, rather than gambling on an unpaid move.
Her **children** age into late adolescence by 2034, although the mortgage remains a concrete pressure.

steps.text: Enroll in a local mechanical certificate if the mine funds course and shifts
Make two extra mortgage principal payments each year before 2034
Keep driving mine shifts while checking the fleet plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade should be enough warning for an honest mine plan. The crew deserves training choices before 2039 robots reach the haul road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, thinking AI may change dispatch, not my hands-on driving first. At 56 in 2039, I can't count on a truck job or assume I can retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and review our mortgage balance with Lila every January. I'd take a mine-funded mechanical course within the next year if the shift pattern permits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy rather than scared right now, because there are years of wages and nearby employers between us and 2039. I don't know what will be available then, so I want options built slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to retire at 56?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't earned a promise like that. The children should be grown by then, but I may still need paid work for the house and ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that decade useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written fleet timetable and paid time to learn something else would let me choose before a notice arrives. I'd trust that more than a speech about everyone having a future.

say: I'd say a **decade** should be enough warning for an honest mine plan.
The crew deserves training choices before **2039 robots** reach the haul road.
think: At 53 in **2036**, thinking AI may change dispatch, not my hands-on driving first.
At 56 in **2039**, I can't count on a truck job or assume I can retire.
do: Keep driving and review our **mortgage balance** with Lila every January.
Take a mine-funded **mechanical course** within the next year if the shift pattern permits.
feel: **Uneasy** about 2039, with time to build options.
S4.quote: At 56 in 2039, I can't count on a truck job or assume I can retire.
fieldNote: The long **runway** lowers immediate income fear without turning a possible robot replacement into a secure retirement date.
She values a written **fleet timetable** and funded learning that fit around continuing paid mine shifts.

steps.text: Keep driving mine shifts and review the mortgage balance each January
Take a mine-funded mechanical course if shift times permit next year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because the 2031 robot date could arrive while our children still depend on us and the mortgage is large. Paid training with real hours and a written fleet plan would help me more than a vague promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a junior driver can get a training place before the experienced people take them all. I'd want the rules written down and the chance to apply while I'm still employed.

headlineQuote: I want a paid apprenticeship now and a wider set of local employers to apply to, rather than only a haul truck licence.
portrait: Amira is a **43-year-old** junior haul truck driver at a large mine, learning routes while earning higher pay.
Her partner, two school-age children and **mortgage** shape every decision, despite more than six months of savings.
She trusts **tested changes** and asks known colleagues to demonstrate route tools before using them.
A fast robot arrival pushes her toward **paid training** and local job applications; more time lets her reduce debt.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 robots could threaten her wage while the children still depend on it.
whatWouldHelp: A written **fleet timetable** and fair access to paid training would let her plan while she remains employed.
